entry.title: Jaeger: Tracing Every Hop of Your Distributed AI Stack

link.title: Jaeger: Tracing Every Hop of Your Distributed AI Stack

entry.content:
Modern AI systems are distributed systems in disguise. A single “ask the model a question” request in a production RAG application usually touches an API gateway, an embedding service, a vector database, a retriever, maybe a reranker, and finally an LLM provider — and if you add agents into the mix, each tool call fans out into further network hops. When a user complains that answers are slow or wrong, a stack trace in one service tells you almost nothing. What you need is a trace: a tree of timed spans showing exactly where the 8 seconds went — 200 ms in retrieval, 6.5 s waiting on the model, 1.2 s re-serializing context you did not need.

That is the problem Jaeger was built to solve. Originally created at Uber and later donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, Jaeger is the most widely deployed open-source distributed tracing platform in the Go ecosystem, and the natural landing zone for traces from an instrumented FastAPI service or any OTel SDK. In 2024 the project shipped Jaeger v2, a fundamental architectural shift: the backend was rebuilt as an OpenTelemetry Collector distribution, so ingestion, sampling, and storage are all expressed as standard OTel components instead of bespoke services. If your app already exports OTLP, retargeting it at Jaeger is usually a one-line environment variable change.

In this post we tour the actual source code of jaegertracing/jaeger on the main branch, following a span from ingest endpoint to rendered UI. Both diagrams below were generated directly from the repository, so every node links to the real source file on GitHub.

Jaeger v2 at a glance: one binary, standard OTel receivers on the left, pluggable storage in the middle, and the query/UI stack on the right, with a standalone remote-storage gRPC server for hybrid deployments.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main(), L12 — the single jaeger binary is an OTel Collector distribution; its entry point just wires factories and executes the command.
  • Components(), L28 — returns the full component set the standard binary ships with, which custom distributions can extend.
  • all-in-one.yaml, L70 — the embedded default configuration accepts OTLP over gRPC on port 4317 and HTTP on 4318, plus legacy Jaeger thrift and Zipkin endpoints.
  • processTraces, L68 — before storage, the adaptive sampling processor recalculates per-operation sampling probabilities from live traffic.
  • TraceWriter, L25 — the write step behind jaeger_storage_exporter: sanitize each OTLP batch, then hand it to the configured backend.
  • GetTraceStoreFactory, L65 — the jaeger_storage extension resolves a named backend into a tracestore.Factory.
  • NewStore, L43 — with no config flags, the binary runs all-in-one against an in-memory store capped at 100,000 traces.
  • NewServer, L57 — the jaeger_query extension binds the HTTP and gRPC query servers on one port.
  • NewQueryService, L129 — the query service wraps any backend reader with search rules, pagination, and archive support.

The detailed map: bootstrap chain, the write path from receivers through the storage exporter, the pluggable backends, the remote-storage gRPC server, and the query/AI surface.

From Install to Your First Trace

The README’s quick start is genuinely two commands long. Run the all-in-one image, which bundles the UI, the collector-side components, the query server, and in-memory storage:

docker run --rm --name jaeger \
  -p 16686:16686 \
  -p 4317:4317 \
  -p 4318:4318 \
  jaegertracing/jaeger:latest

Open http://localhost:16686 for the UI, then point any OpenTelemetry SDK at OTLP gRPC port 4317 or OTLP/HTTP port 4318. If your app already exports OTLP to another backend, you can usually retarget it with one environment variable. Within seconds your service appears in the UI’s service dropdown, and clicking a trace shows the familiar waterfall of spans with per-span timings, tags, logs, and process metadata.

The UI is not the only consumer. The query extension registers a classic JSON API under the default prefix api — see RegisterRoutes, L105 for the route table, including GET /api/traces/{id}, /api/dependencies, and the SPM metrics endpoints. The v2 codebase also serves API v3, an OTLP-native contract: RegisterRoutes, L51 mounts /api/v3/traces and friends on OTLP protobuf types directly, so an LLM analysis tool can consume raw ptrace.Traces without translating Jaeger’s legacy model.

One curl against the JSON API is enough to confirm the flow works headlessly: fetch a trace ID from your app’s tracer output, then curl http://localhost:16686/api/traces/<traceID> and inspect the JSON. Note that in-memory storage means everything evaporates on container restart — fine for development, and the reason production runs swap in a real backend, which we do next.

Inside the v2 Binary: an OTel Collector Distribution

The most interesting thing about Jaeger v2 is what it no longer contains. There is no custom collector daemon: cmd/jaeger builds an OpenTelemetry Collector distribution. main(), L12 calls Components(), L28, which delegates to the registry in cmd/jaeger/internal/components.go — that file registers the OTLP, Jaeger, Zipkin, and Kafka receivers, a set of exporters, and five Jaeger-specific extensions: jaeger_query, jaeger_storage, remote_sampling, expvar, and remotestorage.

Bootstrap behavior lives in NewCommand, L32. The command intercepts the collector’s RunE: if no --config flag was passed, checkConfigAndRun injects the embedded all-in-one.yaml, which is why docker run jaegertracing/jaeger:latest works with zero configuration. Pass your own config and you compose the same components differently — receivers on one port, a tail-sampling processor in the middle, storage elsewhere.

This design is a gift for LLM infrastructure teams. It means one config file describes your whole tracing topology, and the same binary can play collector, query server, or remote-storage role depending on which extensions you enable. Compare that with wiring three separate services, and the appeal for compact Kubernetes deployments becomes obvious.

The Write Path: From Receiver to Storage

Follow a batch of spans inward. After a receiver accepts them, the jaeger_storage_exporter is the last stop. Its TraceWriter, L25 resolves the configured storage at startup in Start, L43 by calling GetTraceStoreFactory, L65, which locates the jaeger_storage extension in the collector host. At runtime, WriteTraces, L112 runs each batch through a sanitizer and forwards it verbatim to the backend.

Everything downstream of that call implements one contract: tracestore.Writer, L14, an OTLP-compatible, idempotent WriteTraces(ctx, td). The interface is documented with unusual care — implementations must write synchronously or explicitly document an asynchronous mode, because the Kafka ingester needs real errors for backpressure and retry. That kind of contract-first thinking is why Jaeger backends stay swappable.

The extension resolves factories lazily in TraceStorageFactory, L184, caching each one, and the shared switch in CreateTraceStorageFactory, L32 maps config to concrete backends. On the v2 storage tree you get: the in-memory store (NewStore, L43, writing via a per-tenant clone at L72), Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (NewFactory, L44, with reader and writer factories at L60 and L66), Cassandra, ClickHouse, Badger, and a gRPC remote backend. Legacy v1 plugins are bridged through adapters like NewTraceWriter, L32, so the long tail of third-party storage plugins keeps working while the ecosystem migrates.

For high-volume deployments the repo ships config variants like config-kafka-collector.yaml and config-kafka-ingester.yaml: collectors export spans into Kafka, and an ingester consumes them into storage. This decouples ingest latency spikes — a burst of agent tool-call traces, say — from your database’s write capacity.

The Read Path: Query APIs, the UI, and MCP Tools for AI Agents

On the serving side, NewServer, L57 builds both an HTTP server and a gRPC server — same port, shared interceptors for bearer tokens and tenancy. registerGRPCHandlers, L98 registers the v2 jaeger.api_v2.QueryService and the v3 service on one gRPC endpoint, and initRouter mounts the API v3 gateway, the classic JSON API, the static UI assets, and a growing set of AI routes.

The domain logic lives in the query service: NewQueryService, L129 wraps any backend reader; GetTraces, L160 fetches by ID; FindTraces, L228 runs searches, normalizing the query in prepareSearchQuery, L280 — which refuses searches without a service name unless the backend advertises support, and enforces time-range bounds. Dependencies for the service graph come from GetDependencies, L569. On the HTTP side, getTrace, L335 is the handler your curl hit earlier.

The genuinely new capability is aimed at agents, not humans. Under /api/ai/, Register, L63 mounts an AI gateway whose MCP endpoint is served by NewHandler, L116 — an MCP server exposing tools like search_traces, get_trace_topology, get_critical_path, and error-root-cause skills over the query service. In other words, your coding agent can now query production traces through the Model Context Protocol the same way it reads files. For anyone building LLM observability alongside evaluation tooling like Opik or workflow analysis with Phoenix, a tracing backend that speaks MCP natively is a meaningful shortcut: the agent gets ground truth about latencies and failures instead of guessed-at logs.

Scaling Out: Remote Storage, Sampling, and Honest Topology Options

Two mechanisms make Jaeger scale beyond one container. First, adaptive sampling: the processor at processTraces, L68 watches operation throughput and adjusts per-route sampling probabilities, served back to SDKs through the remote_sampling extension on ports 5778 (HTTP) and 5779 (gRPC) per the embedded config. High-traffic services send fewer spans; rare operations keep full fidelity.

Second, the remote-storage gRPC server decouples old and new worlds. The v2 binary can embed it via the remotestorage extension — see Start, L37 — and there is also a standalone cmd/remote-storage binary whose NewServer, L40 wraps any backend into gRPC handlers via grpcstorage.NewHandler, L65, registered on the server at L116. The wire contract matches the client factory at NewFactory, L47, whose handler exposes GetTraces, Export, and GetDependencies in handler.go, L48. Practical takeaway: you can keep v1-era agents and collectors in place, front them with a v2 remote-storage pod, and migrate storage underneath without touching application code.

Honest Limits

  • In-memory storage is development-only. The default store caps at 100,000 traces and vanishes on restart. Production requires running Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Cassandra, or ClickHouse — each a real operational commitment. If you only need metrics rather than traces, a time-series stack is far cheaper to operate.
  • Storage costs grow with cardinality. Tracing every LLM call with full prompts and completions as span attributes will bloat Elasticsearch or ClickHouse fast. Sample deliberately, and keep payload blobs in object storage with trace IDs as pointers.
  • v1 to v2 migration is real work. The repo carries both generations — legacy cmd components were removed in v2, but many deployments still run v1 binaries alongside v2 remote storage. Version skew, config translation, and dual-running are documented but non-trivial.
  • Spans are not evaluations. Jaeger tells you what happened and how long it took; it will not tell you whether the model’s answer was good. Pair it with an evaluation layer, and use the new MCP tools as the bridge rather than a replacement.
  • Single-binary mode has no HA story. All-in-one is a single process; meaningful deployments need the collector/query separation (or at least external storage) plus health checks — the config exposes healthcheckv2 on 13133 for exactly that.

For AI engineering teams, the pitch condenses to this: your stack already emits OTLP; Jaeger v2 ingests it with commodity collector config, stores it in whichever database your platform team tolerates, and now — through its MCP server — lets your agents interrogate production latency themselves. That last part is the newest idea in the codebase — and the most likely to change how you debug multi-hop LLM systems.

entry.title: Inside the OpenTelemetry Collector: The Go Engine That Routes Every Trace, Metric and Log

link.title: Inside the OpenTelemetry Collector: The Go Engine That Routes Every Trace, Metric and Log

entry.content:
Modern AI systems are telemetry furnaces. An LLM gateway emits metrics that classic web apps never had: tokens per second, time-to-first-token, queue depth per model replica, cache hit ratios on a prompt store. Every step of an agent — tool call, retrieval hit, retry — wants to be a span. GPU hosts want to report utilization, thermal events and batch occupancy as metrics, and the debugging session that starts with a hallucination usually ends with you reading traces at three in the morning. The hard part is not generating these signals; your frameworks already do. The hard part is moving them: different shapes, different backends, batching under bursty load, retries, tail sampling, redaction of prompts that may contain user data. That plumbing problem is exactly what the OpenTelemetry Collector was built to solve. Its README describes it plainly: a vendor-agnostic implementation of how to receive, process and export telemetry data — one binary that stands between your AI services and every backend you use, from Jaeger to Kafka to a managed vendor.

There are two repositories people conflate. open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector — the subject of this post — is the engine: the component interfaces, the OTLP-native data model, the config system, the service runtime that turns YAML into a directed graph of running components, and the otelcol binary itself. The sibling opentelemetry-collector-contrib repository is the long tail: hundreds of receivers, processors, exporters and connectors, from PostgreSQL scrapers to Kafka brokers. If you have ever added a component to a config file and wondered what actually happens next, the machinery lives in the core repo — and that is the machinery we are going to read, file by file, with line anchors into the main branch.

We will do it in two passes. The overview diagram below follows a signal from the command line to the exporter. The detail diagram then opens every stage up: the collector lifecycle, config resolution, the service graph internals, and the three pdata signal containers. Every symbol mentioned in the text links to the real source, verified in the repo as of today.

Figure 1 — The 10,000-meter view: the otelcol binary builds a Collector, which resolves configuration and hands component factories to the Service, which assembles a directed acyclic graph of receivers, processors and exporters that exchange pdata signals.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • NewCommand, L25 — the cobra root command is the binary’s front door; its RunE constructs a Collector and calls Run.
  • Collector struct, L100 — the process owner: settings, config provider, the Service, state and shutdown channels.
  • ConfigProvider.Get, L55 — serves the configuration on demand and on change.
  • Resolver.Resolve, L164 — fetches each config URI through a provider, merges the maps and expands references.
  • service.New, L108 — builds internal telemetry, extensions and the component graph.
  • graph.Build, L78 — turns the service config into a DAG of component instances.
  • receiverNode, L26 — one graph node per receiver instance, wired to the next consumers.
  • Traces, L21 — the pdata container every component actually passes around.

Figure 2 — The full plumbing: CLI and lifecycle, the confmap resolution stack, the service runtime, the data flow graph with its virtual nodes, and the pdata signal containers that carry your LLM metrics, agent spans and logs.

A Vendor-Agnostic Router, in One Binary

Everything starts in otelcol/. NewCommand, L25 assembles a cobra command whose RunE constructs NewCollector, L129 and then blocks in Collector.Run, L414. Command-line surface is deliberately tiny: flags.go registers the config flag, L15 — repeatable, one location per entry — plus a --set override flag at L39. Two diagnostic subcommands round it out: otelcol components (newComponentsCommand, L45) prints every factory baked into the binary from the Factories, L21 struct, and a validate subcommand (L13) checks a config without running it.

The Collector struct, L100 walks through four states, StateStarting through StateClosed (L30), and its Run method is just a startup call followed by a select loop: it waits on the config watcher (L464), on asynchronous component errors, on SIGHUP/SIGINT/SIGTERM, and on the channel closed by Collector.Shutdown, L166. Config change or reload signal triggers reloadConfiguration, L289, which tears down the retiring Service and builds a new one — with a partial-reload fast path (UpdateReceivers, L273) that restarts only the receivers that actually changed and leaves the rest of the graph untouched. For a long-running AI gateway this means you can tune processors without dropping in-flight signals.

The Config Layer: From a URI to a Struct

The Collector never reads files itself. ConfigProvider, L23 wraps a confmap.Resolver and exposes Get/Watch/Shutdown. Inside the resolver, Resolve, L164 retrieves each configured location through a pluggable Provider interface, L54, merges the resulting maps in order, runs converters, and expands references like ${env:OTEL_KEY}. The scheme dispatch is the elegant part: a file provider whose scheme is literally “file”, L18, an env provider, L21, plus http/https and yaml providers out of the box. Watching is symmetric: Resolver.Watch, L258 returns a channel that fires when any watched location changes.

The resolved map is unmarshalled into otelcol.Config, L22 — top-level maps for receivers, exporters, processors, connectors and extensions, plus the service section — and validated by Config.Validate, L49: an empty file is an error, at least one receiver and one exporter must be configured, and every component referenced by the service section must exist. Fail here and the process exits before any component is built.

The Service Graph: A DAG, Not a Chain

This is the part most people get wrong about the Collector. It is not a linear chain; it is a directed acyclic graph, assembled at runtime by the service/internal/graph package. service.New, L108 first creates the internal telemetry (resource, logger, meter and tracer providers), then calls initGraph, L340, which feeds builders and the configured signal flows into graph.Build, L78.

Build runs three phases. createNodes, L101 adds one node per component instance — receivers and exporters are deduplicated across flows of the same signal, processors are unique per flow, and connectors (connectorNode, L31) are type-checked so an exporter on one signal always pairs with a receiver on another. createEdges, L268 then wires each flow: receivers emit into a virtual capabilitiesNode, L20 that aggregates whether the flow mutates data, the processors are chained in config order, and a fanOutNode, L15 sits before the exporters so one signal can fan out to many backends. Finally buildComponents, L297 topologically sorts the graph (topo.Sort, L298) and instantiates real components in reverse order, handing each one its nextConsumers, L378 — this is the moment a receiver receives the consumer it will push spans into.

Startup respects the DAG: StartAll, L406 starts downstream components first so every consumer is ready before its producer (Service.Start, L232 starts extensions, then the graph, then logs the famous “Everything is ready” line), and ShutdownAll, L467 stops in the opposite order so components drain cleanly. The Host, L31 ties it together as the component.Host implementation, answering factory lookups (GetFactory, L48), status reporting and zPages.

From Install to Your First Model

From install to first flowing signal takes about five minutes, and it doubles as a working mental model of the whole machine — your first model of how telemetry moves.

  1. Download a distro binary. The README links the releases page, where the project publishes signed artifacts (cosign verification is documented in the README). Container images otel/opentelemetry-collector are published under the same release process.
  2. Write a minimal config. One OTLP receiver (gRPC on 4317, HTTP on 4318) and the debug exporter are the classic starting pair:
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
exporters:
  debug:
    verbosity: detailed
service:
  telemetry:
    logs:
      level: info
  # under the service section you also declare your signal flows:
  # for each of traces, metrics and logs, list which receivers feed
  # which exporters, with optional processors between them.
  # The getting-started guide shows the exact stanza.
  1. Run it: otelcol --config=config.yaml. The config flag is the one requirement — command.go rejects a start without it, L61. For the precise service stanza, the official getting-started guide (linked from the README) walks through the exact flow declaration.
  2. Push one signal through. Any OTLP client will do — curl a JSON span to port 4318, or point a Python opentelemetry-sdk tracer at it. The debug exporter prints the pdata you just created, and you can literally watch your span travel receiver → capabilities node → fan-out → exporter, exactly as the diagram promised.

For an AI stack this scales up naturally: point your LLM gateway’s OTLP endpoint at the Collector, add a batch processor to absorb traffic spikes, and export metrics to Prometheus, traces to Jaeger, or mirror raw signals onto Kafka when a downstream consumer wants its own replay. Same binary, same graph, one config file.

pdata: Where Every Signal Lives

Every component in that graph speaks one in-memory language: pdata. The package doc says it directly — pdata defines the data model for all supported signals, L6. It is a hand-written Go mirror of the OTLP protobufs: Traces, L21 is a wrapper around resource-span slices (ResourceSpans, L49), Logs, L21 and Metrics, L21 follow the same resource → scope → record layering, and pcommon.Map, L18 with Range, L242 is the attribute bag they all share, alongside a fixed-size TraceID, L15. At the wire edge, ExportRequest, L17 wraps a Traces value for gRPC/HTTP transport without re-copying the data.

Why does a dedicated model matter? Because signals cross many component boundaries on their way through the graph, and re-serializing at each hop would be ruinous. pdata lets a receiver hand a mutable structure to a processor and on to an exporter with zero copies of the payload between them — but mutability is tracked: the capabilities node computes whether anything downstream mutates data, and the receiver side clones defensively when it does. When you build AI-specific processors (prompt redaction, token-cost attribution, trace sampling by latency), this is the API you write against, and the graph wiring is what guarantees your processor sees every signal exactly once.

Honest Limits

  • The core repo has no AI-specific components. Batching, tail sampling or prompt-scrubbing processors live in contrib (or in your own Go module). The core gives you the framework and a small stable set; the catalog is a separate dependency decision.
  • The service stanza is mandatory and strict. Validation requires at least one receiver and one exporter, and every reference must resolve — the empty-config errors are right there in config.go, L17.
  • The graph package is internal by design. You extend the Collector by implementing factories and components, not by editing the DAG; the flow shape is data-driven from config, which is a feature but also a constraint if you wanted exotic topologies.
  • The code moves fast. Every anchor in this post was verified against main on 2026-11-01; line numbers will drift, symbols less so. Treat the links as a snapshot.
  • No benchmarks here on purpose. The README’s own claims are qualitative — usable, performant, observable, extensible, unified — and I see no reason to invent numbers the project did not make.
  • Self-observability is real but easy to forget. The Host registers zPages endpoints (RegisterZPages, L110, rendering via HandleZPages, L21) that show the live graph and component status — turn them on before you need them at 3 a.m.

That is the whole journey: a cobra command, a config resolver, a graph builder, and a data model — four ideas that together route every trace, metric and log your AI stack will ever emit.

entry.title: Thanos: Giving Prometheus Unlimited Memory with Go and Object Storage

link.title: Thanos: Giving Prometheus Unlimited Memory with Go and Object Storage

entry.content:
If you run even a modest AI or ML fleet, your metrics outgrow your monitoring faster than your models outgrow your GPUs. A single GPU export loop that scrapes utilization, memory pressure, KV-cache occupancy and request latency every fifteen seconds generates millions of samples per series per year. Keep thirty days locally and every interesting question — what did peak inference latency look like during last quarter’s rollout, how did GPU thermal throttling drift across the summer, which experiment batch saturated the network — becomes unanswerable. Long-horizon telemetry is not a nice-to-have for machine learning systems; it is the training data for your capacity planning, your autoscaling rules and your postmortems.

Thanos exists for exactly this gap. The project describes itself as “a set of components that can be composed into a highly available metric system with unlimited storage capacity, which can be added seamlessly on top of existing Prometheus deployments.” It is a CNCF Incubating project written in Go, and its core trick is pragmatic: it keeps using the Prometheus 2.0 storage format — two-hour TSDB blocks — and simply makes those blocks durable in any object store, from S3 to MinIO, while layering on global querying, deduplication, downsampling and horizontal scaling.

What makes Thanos worth a source tour is that it is not one monolith but a constellation of small, composable processes, each with one job, all speaking one shared gRPC contract. In this post we walk the actual Go source — the block metadata model, the store gateway that serves bucket data, the compactor that rewrites history, the fan-out query layer, the rule evaluator and the stateless receive component that ingests remote writes — and map how they fit together. We read from the main branch of thanos-io/thanos throughout.

Overview: Prometheus sidecars and receive nodes push immutable blocks into object storage; the store gateway serves them via the Store API; the querier fans out across every endpoint behind a caching frontend; the compactor and ruler run as side operations.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts as one binary. The entrypoint in main, L44 describes itself as “a block storage based long-term storage for Prometheus”, and lines 56–63 register all eight subcommands — sidecar, store, query, rule, compact, tools, receive and query-frontend — so one Docker image covers the whole deployment.
  • The sidecar is the classic starting point. registerSidecar, L61 wires a process that sits next to Prometheus, proxies its data through the Store API, and when a bucket is configured, continuously uploads new TSDB blocks.
  • Uploads are handled by the shipper: Shipper.Sync, L344 scans the local data directory and pushes blocks into the bucket, while Shipper.upload, L478 does the actual transfer.
  • Every block is self-describing. The Meta, L66 struct carries the block’s ULID, min/max time, statistics and external labels — the glue that lets any component decide which block is relevant to a query.
  • On the serving side, the store gateway is BucketStore, L395: it syncs block metadata from the bucket and answers Series, L1560 requests by streaming chunks straight from object storage.
  • To keep the object store from melting under hot queries, index reads pass through CachingBucket, L39, which memoizes index and chunk-range reads in memory, memcached or Redis.
  • The query layer is where Thanos becomes “global”. EndpointSet, L255 tracks every Store API endpoint, and the fan-out querier around querier, L143 merges results from all of them in parallel, deduplicating replica pairs on the fly.
  • Two side processes keep history tidy and alerting global: the compactor, whose Syncer, L55 watches the bucket and rewrites overlapping blocks, and the ruler, whose Manager, L117 evaluates recording and alerting rules against the global view.

Detail view: the block fetcher and metadata model that all components share, the store gateway's lazy index readers and caching, the frontend's splitting and sharding tripperware, and the compactor's planner, downsampler and retention passes.

The Block Format That Everything Shares

The reason Thanos can scale is a data model choice, not a service mesh. Prometheus periodically cuts its head data into immutable, compressed two-hour blocks, each with a compact index and chunk files. Thanos treats those blocks as the unit of storage, replication and retention — upload them once and every other component only ever reads. The service Store, L26 definition in pkg/store/storepb/rpc.proto is the shared gRPC contract: a Series RPC that streams matching time series, plus LabelNames and LabelValues for discovery. Sidecars, store gateways and receive nodes all implement it, which is why the querier does not care whether data is twenty seconds old in a sidecar or five years old in a bucket.

Listing the bucket is consequently a critical path. NewMetaFetcher, L403 builds a concurrent metadata fetcher that lists block directories, downloads each meta.json, and passes it through a chain of filters — consistency delay, deletion marks, duplicate detection — before anyone trusts it. The store gateway then opens each block lazily: LazyBinaryReader, L70 memory-maps the index header only when a query actually touches that block, which is how a single gateway can serve terabytes without holding everything in RAM. Per-block series selection lives in the bucketBlock, L2431 machinery of pkg/store/bucket.go, with chunk readers that fetch and decompress on demand.

From Install to Your First Global Query

The fastest verified path uses the official image published at quay.io/thanos/thanos on every commit to main, with minor releases every six weeks. Assume Prometheus is already running locally and you have a bucket config file for your object store — S3, GCS, Azure or MinIO all work through the same YAML shape.

First, attach a sidecar to Prometheus and start backing data up:

thanos sidecar \
    --tsdb.path            /var/prometheus \
    --prometheus.url       "http://localhost:9090" \
    --objstore.config-file bucket_config.yaml

That command, straight from the project’s quick tutorial, ships every new block to the bucket and simultaneously exposes a Store API on port 19090 backed by the live Prometheus data. Give every Prometheus instance a globally unique set of external labels (for example replica: A on one and replica: B on its HA twin) — this is mandatory, because those labels are how data from different instances is later told apart and merged.

Next, point a stateless querier at all your Store API endpoints:

thanos query \
    --http-address 0.0.0.0:19192 \
    --endpoint     1.2.3.4:19090 \
    --endpoint     1.2.3.5:19090 \
    --endpoint     dnssrv+_grpc._tcp.thanos-store.monitoring.svc

Endpoints can be static, DNS A records (dns+) or SRV records (dnssrv+). Open the UI on port 19192 and you can run one PromQL query across every connected Prometheus at once; add --query.replica-label replica and the querier transparently deduplicates the HA pairs. Because the querier implements the Prometheus HTTP API, Grafana can point at it unchanged. Once your historical data is in the bucket, run a store gateway (thanos store --data-dir /var/thanos/store --objstore.config-file bucket_config.yaml), register its endpoint the same way, and years of data appear in the same query. Finally, a singleton compactor (thanos compact --data-dir /var/thanos/compact --objstore.config-file bucket_config.yaml) keeps the bucket compacted and downsampled. For Kubernetes fleets, the kube-thanos manifests and the Prometheus Operator integration package all of this into standard workloads.

Compaction, Downsampling and Retention

Blocks in a bucket do not compact themselves. The compactor is a single-instance process that periodically lists the bucket with the same MetaFetcher, L712 machinery as everyone else, groups overlapping blocks by their external labels, and rewrites each group into progressively larger time ranges. The rewrite itself is delegated to a second-generation engine: Compactor.WriteSeries, L77 in pkg/compactv2 merges overlapping block contents through a streaming series writer, while the tsdbBasedPlanner, L23 decides which blocks are due for the next compaction level.

Two extra passes make long histories queryable. The downsampler builds coarse 5-minute and 1-hour resolutions of every block — Downsample, L73 aggregates raw chunks into counters-with-resets and averaged histograms — and the query layer automatically picks a resolution matching the step of your query. Retention is symmetric: ApplyRetentionPolicyByResolution, L25 marks blocks whose max time falls outside the configured window for each resolution, and the BlocksCleaner, L26 physically deletes marked blocks from the bucket. The result is a storage hierarchy where a year-long dashboard hits 1h-downsampled data while a five-minute incident review hits raw blocks.

Ingestion at Scale with Receive

Sidecars are perfect when Prometheus owns the data, but what if you need to push telemetry in — from federated clusters, from jobs that speak the remote-write protocol, from other remote-write compatible sources? The receive component is a stateless, horizontally scalable ingestion tier. Incoming writes hit Handler, L142, which validates and routes each request through a Hashring, L60 — a consistent-hash ring over receive nodes — so every tenant’s series lands on exactly one responsible node, with configurable replication factor fanning copies to peers.

The responsible node appends through Writer.Write, L74 into one of several local TSDBs owned by MultiTSDB, L55, a storage multiplexer that isolates tenants and uploads each tenant’s blocks to the bucket via its own shipper. Because every receive node also exposes the Store API, the querier sees ingested data the same way it sees sidecar data — no special casing anywhere in the query path. If you already push samples into Prometheus remote write, receive is a drop-in escalation path from single-instance to distributed ingestion.

Honest Limits

Thanos is infrastructure, not magic, and the sharp edges are worth naming before you deploy it:

  • Compactor is a singleton by design. The documentation is explicit that it must run as a single instance and must not run concurrently with manual bucket modifications; two compactors racing over the same bucket is the classic operational footgun.
  • Global queries are only as fast as their slowest endpoint. The fan-out querier merges responses in parallel, but one misbehaving store gateway or sidecar inflates every cross-cluster query. Partial response strategies exist, but they trade completeness for latency.
  • Query cost grows with label cardinality, not just time range. Downsampling makes long-range dashboards cheap, but high-cardinality series still dominate index lookups; sharding and frontend caching (NewTripperware, L37) mitigate rather than eliminate this.
  • External labels are load-bearing. A collision between two Prometheus instances’ external labels leads to overlapping blocks in the bucket, and untangling that is painful. Set them before the first upload, not after.
  • The object store is now a production dependency. Latency and rate limits of your bucket tier propagate into query latencies; budget a real storage backend rather than treating it as cold archive.

For teams that want object-storage-backed metrics without a component zoo, alternatives like VictoriaMetrics take a more monolithic route — we compared that trade-off in our VictoriaMetrics source tour. For Kubernetes-native fleets that already run Prometheus sidecars, though, Thanos’s block-first design in about a hundred thousand lines of Go remains the reference architecture for “query any window, any replica, one PromQL”.

entry.title: VictoriaMetrics: Reading the Go Source of a Time-Series Powerhouse

link.title: VictoriaMetrics: Reading the Go Source of a Time-Series Powerhouse

entry.content:
Anyone who has trained or served a model at scale knows the feeling: the GPU node is hot, the loss curve looks fine, and then the run silently stalls because some unattended metric — host memory, NVLink errors, an overloaded datadog-sidecar — drifted for twenty minutes and nobody saw it. Modern AI/ML infrastructure is a firehose of telemetry: per-GPU utilization and temperature, training-step latency, token throughput, queue depths on inference servers, cache hit ratios on a serving fleet. Every one of those signals is a time series, and the tool you pick to store and query them decides whether you find problems in minutes or after the cluster melts. That is the niche a purpose-built time-series database (TSDB) lives in, and it is why Prometheus and its storage backends matter so much to ML platform teams.

VictoriaMetrics is one of the most interesting open-source TSDBs in this space. Written almost entirely in Go by Aliaksandr Valialkin and the VictoriaMetrics company, it presents itself as “a fast, cost-effective, and scalable solution for monitoring and managing time series data”, and it ships in two flavors the project README explicitly open-sources: a single-node version and a cluster version. It speaks the Prometheus remote-write protocol natively, doubles as long-term storage for Prometheus, works as a drop-in data source for Grafana, and also ingests InfluxDB line protocol, Graphite plaintext, OpenTSDB, DataDog, OpenTelemetry, CSV, and JSON line formats. The README’s case-study page lists users like Grammarly, Roblox, Wix, and Spotify, which is a decent hint that this codebase has survived contact with real production traffic.

What makes it worth a source tour, though, is not the marketing line — it is how clean the architecture is once you descend past the HTTP layer. The whole storage engine lives in a single package, lib/storage, and the two service halves (ingestion and query) live in app/vminsert and app/vmselect. On the current master branch the single-node binary in app/victoria-metrics wires all three together in one process, which makes the entire system readable end-to-end in an afternoon. This post walks that path with two interactive diagrams, and every code link below points at a symbol I verified in the tree at commit level, so you can click through and read along.

Overview: how writers, the single-node binary, the three internal services, and the lib/storage core fit together. Nodes link straight to the source files on GitHub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Writers enter through vmagent’s main, L105, a standalone agent that scrapes or receives metrics and pushes them over remote write; its sharding client lives in client, L92.
  • The single-node binary victoria-metrics main, L99 explicitly calls vmstorage.Init, vmselect.Init, and vminsert.Init in sequence — three services composed into one process, served on the default port :8428.
  • On the ingestion side, the router in vminsert main.go, L171 accepts /prometheus/api/v1/write and /api/v1/push among many protocol endpoints, then hands rows to the shared buffer type InsertCtx, L52.
  • FlushBufs, L275 is the moment buffered rows become storage rows: it applies relabeling, stream aggregation, then calls VMInsertAPI.WriteRows at line 292.
  • The storage app opens the engine in vmstorage Init, L123 via storage.MustOpenStorage on the -storageDataPath directory, and publishes the insert API handle at L200.
  • The engine entrypoint Storage.AddRows, L1659 batches incoming MetricRow values; the read mirror is Storage.SearchTSIDs, L1270.
  • Below that, the table in table.go, L300 (MustAddRows) routes each raw row to the partition owning its timestamp’s month.
  • Each month of data is a partition with its own background compressor: mergeParts, L1234 continuously folds small parts into bigger ones.
  • Filters are resolved by the inverted index: indexDB.SearchTSIDs, L1934 turns label matchers into time-series IDs.

Detail view: the ingestion relays, the PromQL/MetricsQL query path, and the parts-and-blocks machinery inside lib/storage, with verified line anchors.

From Install to Your First Metrics Query

Getting a running server is deliberately boring, which is a feature. Grab a prebuilt binary from the GitHub releases page (or a Docker image such as victoriametrics/victoria-metrics from Docker Hub — both are linked from the README), and start it with a data directory:

./victoria-metrics-prod -storageDataPath=/var/data/vm -retentionPeriod=1

Both flags are real and verified in source: -storageDataPath is declared with the default victoria-metrics-data in vmstorage main.go, L29, and -retentionPeriod (default one month) in L30. The server listens on :8428 unless -httpListenAddr says otherwise — that default is hardcoded in the binary’s main, L93.

You have two ways to get data in. The quick one: the single-node binary embeds its own scraper. It accepts a standard Prometheus scrape config via -promscrape.config (the flag is validated by the -dryRun mode of the main binary), so you can point it straight at exporters or DCGM/DCGM-exporter endpoints on your GPU boxes and skip Prometheus entirely for small setups. The scale-out one: point your existing Prometheus remote_write block, or vmagent, at http://<host>:8428/api/v1/write — the endpoint set is dispatched in vminsert’s RequestHandler, L171, and the snappy-protobuf decoding for that exact endpoint happens in promremotewrite InsertHandler, L23.

Then query it. Open http://localhost:8428/vmui (the built-in UI, routed at vmselect main.go, L454) or hit the API directly:

curl 'http://localhost:8428/api/v1/query' \
  -d 'query=sum(rate(DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL[5m])) by (gpu)'

The /api/v1/query and /api/v1/query_range routes are registered in vmselect main.go, L207 and L216. VictoriaMetrics accepts both PromQL and its own superset dialect, MetricsQL, so dashboards you already built for Grafana keep working unchanged. If you have never wired a TSDB to Grafana before, the flow is identical to what you’d do with TimescaleDB or ClickHouse as a data source — point the datasource at the HTTP endpoint, pick the query language, build panels.

The Storage Core: Tables, Partitions, and Parts

The heart of the system is lib/storage. The top-level Storage object (opened at MustOpenStorage, L183) owns a table, and the table is time-partitioned: one partition per calendar month. That choice drives everything else. Writes arrive as batches at table.MustAddRows, L300, which sorts rows by timestamp and hands each batch to the owning partition — the partition object is created in newPartition, L296.

Inside a partition, data lives in immutable “parts”. Fresh samples first accumulate in RAM as an inmemoryPart, L15, then get flushed to an on-disk part (part, L30) described by a small metadata header (partHeader, L19). A part stores columnar blocks, L22 — chunks of TSIDs, timestamps, and values that are compressed independently. Merging is where retention and dedup happen almost for free: the background merger at mergeParts, L1234 streams several parts through a k-way merge in mergeBlockStreams, L19, drops anything older than the retention deadline via skipSamplesOutsideRetention, L205, and collapses duplicates with DeduplicateSamples, L30. Because every merge rewrites data anyway, retention is not a separate deletion sweep — it is a side effect of the normal compaction the engine already has to do. That is the kind of design decision that only becomes obvious when you read the code rather than the docs.

The Inverted Index That Makes Filters Cheap

A TSDB’s real challenge is not storing numbers; it is answering “give me every series where job=gpu-exporter and model=A100” without scanning the world. VictoriaMetrics solves this with a per-partition inverted index in index_db.go. The indexDB struct is defined at L77, opened by mustOpenIndexDB, L168, and populated when new series register their global and per-day index entries in createGlobalIndexes, L415. Series identity is modeled by MetricName, L137 (metric group plus tag pairs), marshaled into key material for the index; query-time matchers are compiled from TagFilters, L160 into set operations over metric IDs.

The per-day aspect is the subtle bit: the index is partially sharded by day so that searches only touch the days in the requested time range, and the resolver entry point is indexDB.SearchTSIDs, L1934. Once TSIDs are known, the data side takes over: a SearchQuery, L323 is executed by the streaming Search, L166 object, which merges results across partitions through tableSearch, L62 and per-partition iterators.

Querying: MetricsQL on Top of Streaming Blocks

The query side is a clean layering. HTTP routes in vmselect hand the raw query string to Exec, L37, which parses the expression (with a parse cache), evaluates it, and normalizes results. The evaluator core is evalExpr, L257, parameterized by an EvalConfig, L116 that carries deadlines, concurrency limits, and a query tracer. Raw data materialization happens at netstorage.ProcessSearchQuery, L1090 — called from the evaluator at eval.go L1834 — which fans the search across workers and merges compressed blocks into Result objects (Result, L45).

Two nice touches deserve mention. First, the rollup function library — everything like rate, avg_over_time, and a pile of extras beyond stock PromQL — lives in one giant file; the plain ones are as readable as rollupAvg, L1541. Second, rollup results are cached persistently on disk and invalidated on restarts, set up by InitRollupResultCache, L119; for dashboards re-rendering the same GPU-utilization window every five seconds, that cache is what keeps query latency flat. Note that on this unified master, the single-node binary calls all three services in-process — the cluster version, documented separately by the project, splits them into independently scalable services, which the README states is also open source under Apache 2.0.

Why AI/ML Teams Should Care

For ML platform work, three properties matter more than raw ingest speed. High-cardinality tolerance: per-GPU, per-step, per-experiment tags multiply series counts brutally, and VictoriaMetrics’ index design (global plus per-day entries, plus a cardinality limiter flag on the insert path) is built for exactly that. Operational cheapness: one Go binary, no dependencies, snapshot-based backups — you can run it beside a single training node or centralize a fleet. And ecosystem compatibility: remote write means your existing Prometheus alerting and Grafana boards keep working, and the multi-protocol relays mean training frameworks emitting InfluxDB-style or OpenTSDB-style metrics do not need rewrites. The project README reports substantial performance and compression advantages over competing systems; I have not benchmarked those claims here, so treat them as the vendor’s numbers, not mine — but the architecture you just walked through is consistent with them: columnar blocks, aggressive merging, and an index that shrinks query fan-out.

Honest Limits

Reading the source also exposes the trade-offs. The unified master branch is a fast-moving target — the storage package has recently grown legacy-compat files (storage_legacy.go, index_db_legacy.go) and the single-node/cluster split has been reorganized into shared packages, so blog-level line anchors age faster here than in quieter codebases. Query concurrency is deliberately capped (the main binary computes a conservative default of 2x CPU cores capped at 16), because one heavy range query can saturate cores — you need capacity planning, not just a bigger box. Retention and dedup happen during merges, which means aggressive -retentionPeriod changes or dedup settings apply gradually, not instantly. And while ingestion speaks many protocols, it is not a general-purpose analytical database: there is no SQL, no joins across arbitrary tables — if your telemetry needs heavy ad-hoc analytics, pairing VictoriaMetrics for metrics with ClickHouse for events, or using Kafka to fan out between them, is a common pattern. For long-term object storage of raw backups, the separate vmbackup tool targets S3-compatible stores such as MinIO. Know what the tool is for, and it is excellent at that.

entry.title: Kafka Under the Hood: How the Distributed Commit Log Actually Works

link.title: Kafka Under the Hood: How the Distributed Commit Log Actually Works

entry.content:
Every AI system eventually hits the same wall: your models are only as good, and only as fresh, as the events that reach them. Feature vectors generated a few seconds after a user click, GPU utilization samples scraped off a training node, inference requests and their latencies, token-by-token usage records from an LLM gateway — all of these arrive as continuous streams of facts, and batching them through cron jobs or message queues that silently drop data stops scaling fast. This is the gap Apache Kafka was built to fill, and it is why Kafka sits upstream of so many ML feature stores, real-time dashboards, and telemetry backends (often right next to a columnar sink like ClickHouse).

Kafka’s core idea is deceptively simple: a distributed, append-only commit log. Producers append records to the end of partitioned logs; consumers read them at their own pace by keeping an offset — a pointer into the log — rather than by deleting messages. Because the log is durable and replayable, the same stream can feed a live dashboard, a training-data dump into object storage, and an online feature extractor simultaneously, each with its own position. Fault tolerance comes from replicating each partition across brokers, with a high-watermark defining what has been safely copied and therefore what consumers are allowed to see.

In this post we read the actual implementation on the trunk branch of apache/kafka — the Scala/Java broker core plus its Java clients. Two architecture diagrams follow: a high-level overview, and a detailed map of the classes that carry every message from a producer’s send() call to a consumer’s poll(). All class and line references link into the real sources on GitHub, so you can follow along in your editor.

Overview: records flow from the producer's accumulator through the Sender to the broker's network layer, get dispatched by KafkaApis to the ReplicaManager, land in the UnifiedLog as indexed segments, while the group coordinator tracks consumers. Click any node to open the source on GitHub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • KafkaProducer.send, L1027 serializes the record, runs it through interceptors, and picks a destination partition — either one you set, or computed in partition() at L1681.
  • RecordAccumulator.drain, L1083 collects the batches that are ready to go, capped by the max request size per node.
  • Sender.run, L241 is the producer’s I/O loop; it turns drained batches into ProduceRequest RPCs via sendProduceRequest, L896.
  • SocketServer, L71 accepts connections with an Acceptor (L458) and reads and decodes requests in Processor threads (L779), enqueueing them into a bounded queue.
  • KafkaRequestHandler.run, L108 pulls requests off that queue and dispatches them at L167 to the API layer.
  • KafkaApis.handleProduceRequest, L401 is the protocol facade every client request crosses; fetches enter at handleFetchRequest, L568.
  • ReplicaManager.appendRecordsToLeader, L586 checks the ISR and required acks, then routes the write through a Partition to the log.
  • UnifiedLog.appendAsLeader, L1033 appends to the active segment and rolls it when it grows too large (maybeRoll, L2166).
  • GroupCoordinatorService.joinGroup, L1009 runs consumer-group rebalancing and offset commits on the new KRaft-era coordinator runtime.

Detail: the producer's accumulator–Sender–NetworkClient chain, the consumer's delegate split (classic vs KIP-848 async), the broker's network/handler/replication tiers, the segment-and-index storage engine, and the coordinator's service–shard–metadata split.

The Broker: From Socket to Commit Log

The request path is deliberately boring, which is why it is fast. SocketServer (class at L71) multiplexes NIO sockets: one Acceptor per listener (L458) hands new connections to Processor threads (L779) that decrypt, parse frame headers, and enqueue complete requests. A fixed pool of KafkaRequestHandler worker threads — sized by num.io.threads and resizable at runtime through KafkaRequestHandlerPool, L227 — drains the queue held by RequestChannel, L40, and replies travel back through sendResponse, L91.

KafkaApis (class, L95) is the switchboard: produce requests go to handleProduceRequest (L401), fetches to handleFetchRequest (L568), offset reads to handleOffsetFetchRequest (L1029), and group membership to handleJoinGroupRequest (L1390). Each handler validates the request, calls into the right subsystem, and registers a callback that completes the response asynchronously — the handler thread is never blocked waiting for a disk write or a quorum ack.

The replication brain lives in ReplicaManager (class, L154). appendRecordsToLeader (L586) refuses writes if the partition has no elected leader or the ISR has shrunk below min.insync.replicas; the actual append funnels through appendToLocalLog (L1376) into per-partition state held by Partition (class, L163). Leadership transitions are explicit — makeLeader (L590) and makeFollower (L696) — triggered by metadata records from the KRaft controller. Reads flow through fetchMessages (L1665), which can park a fetch and defer the response until enough new data arrives, a trick that keeps consumer latency low without busy polling.

The Storage Engine: Segments, Indexes, Watermarks

One of the bigger architectural shifts of recent Kafka versions is that the log implementation moved from Scala into a plain-Java storage module. The Scala kafka.log.LogManager you find in core is now just a factory (object, L34) that instantiates the Java org.apache.kafka.storage.internals.log.LogManager (class, L81). That Java class owns the log-directory map — getOrCreateLog at L1239 maps a TopicPartition to its UnifiedLog — and background jobs for retention, flushing, and recovery that kick off in startup() at L771.

UnifiedLog (class, L105) is the per-partition commit log. Leader-side appends go through appendAsLeader (L1033), which validates record offsets, updates the leader epoch, and assigns contiguous offsets; follower-side replication enters via appendAsFollower (L1093). The write itself is delegated to LocalLog (class, L71), whose append at L586 writes into the active segment, and whose flush at L265 fsyncs up to a given offset — this flush boundary is what the recovery-point checkpoint tracks.

Each segment pairs a data file with two sparse indexes. LogSegment (class, L65) decides when to roll with shouldRoll (L167) — segment bytes reached, time rolled over, or index full — and appends records at L250, indexing the first record’s position per write call. The data file is FileRecords (class, L45, note the new record.internal package) backed by a memory-mapped file; append at L249 is just a write at the end, and truncateTo at L321 is what makes unclean leader elections recoverable. OffsetIndex (lookup, L97) maps relative offsets to file positions with binary search, and TimeIndex (class, L54) does the same for timestamps, enabling time-based retention and “read from yesterday 10:00” seeks. Idempotent and transactional producers are tracked by ProducerStateManager (class, L70), which persists sequence numbers as periodic snapshots (loadSnapshots, L184).

The high-watermark is the bridge between replication and visibility: UnifiedLog.highWatermark (L506) reports the largest offset replicated to all in-sync replicas, and the log only exposes records below it to consumers. Log-end sits at L2142; everything between watermark and log-end is written but not yet safe.

Clients: Producers and Consumers

KafkaProducer (class, L251) is a bookkeeping front end for a background machine. Both send overloads (L1027 and L1147) funnel into doSend (L1180), which serializes the key and value, waits up to max.block.ms for partition metadata, and appends the record into a ProducerBatch via tryAppend, L168. Batching is the producer’s main performance lever: linger.ms lets batches fill, batch.size caps them, and compression applies per batch. The Sender thread then drains and ships them, tracking in-flight batches for retries and sequencing.

KafkaConsumer (class, L552) is now a thin facade over two delegates. subscribe (L725) joins a group; poll (L987) simply forwards to whichever protocol you run. The classic delegate (ClassicKafkaConsumer, L117, poll at L657) uses the long-standing group protocol with heartbeats on a background thread; the newer AsyncKafkaConsumer (class, L178, poll at L936) implements the KIP-848 server-side rebalance protocol, moving most rebalance work out of a global lock. Both paths collect completed fetches into ordered records through FetchCollector (class, L51) and talk to the broker via ConsumerNetworkClient (send, L107), which wraps the shared NetworkClient, L89 — the same I/O core the producer uses, with send at L616 and a completion poll at L705. If you have ever wired Kafka into an Airflow DAG, this split matters: the consumer’s poll loop is where streaming and batch worlds hand off.

Group Coordination: The New Java Runtime

Consumer groups have historically been managed by a Scala coordinator embedded in the broker. On trunk that logic lives in a dedicated group-coordinator module. GroupCoordinatorService (class, L166) is the RPC surface — joinGroup at L1009, syncGroup at L1150, heartbeat at L1193, and commitOffsets at L2352 — all returning futures rather than blocking handler threads.

Internally the service routes each group to a shard keyed by the group’s partition in the coordinator’s log, and GroupCoordinatorShard (class, L158) is a deterministic state machine: membership changes and offset commits are first written as records, then applied to in-memory state, which makes group state reproducible after restarts — the same write-ahead-log philosophy as the log itself. Offset bookkeeping ends in OffsetMetadataManager (class, L80), whose commitOffset at L620 produces the records that back the well-known __consumer_offsets topic.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s quickstart path is KRaft-only — no ZooKeeper. To build from source, run ./gradlew jar, then bootstrap a single-node cluster exactly as the README shows:

KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID="$(./bin/kafka-storage.sh random-uuid)"
./bin/kafka-storage.sh format --standalone -t $KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID -c config/server.properties
./bin/kafka-server-start.sh config/server.properties

That is a real KRaft controller and broker in one JVM: the storage tool stamps a cluster ID into the metadata log, and the server starts from config/server.properties. From there the official quickstart at kafka.apache.org/quickstart walks you through creating a topic with bin/kafka-topics.sh and exercising the round trip with the console producer and consumer — a two-minute verification before you write any code.

For an AI workload, the natural next step is making your first event a model-relevant one: emit inference requests as JSON keyed by user ID, append feature updates from your training jobs, or ship GPU telemetry from every node. A Python producer (pip install kafka-python-ng or confluent-kafka) needs only bootstrap servers and a topic name to start appending; the durable log means a consumer that crashes loses nothing, it just resumes from its last committed offset. That replay property is what makes Kafka a good complement to Prometheus — metrics answer “how is the system now,” while the log answers “give me every event since last Tuesday.” And when the stream grows into a lake, the same events can be batch-drained to object storage or queried directly in ClickHouse for offline analysis.

Honest Limits

Kafka is not a database: there are no secondary indexes, no queries, no per-key updates — the OffsetIndex exists to reach a position in a file, nothing more. Retention is a blunt instrument configured in LogConfig (class, L65) — time- or size-based deletion of whole segments — so random access to old records is what compaction and external stores are for. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition; choosing a good partition key for your events is a real design decision, and rekeying after the fact is painful. A broker JVM with modest defaults is fine to start with, but cross-AZ replication traffic, segment fsync tuning, and partition counts that now also drive KRaft metadata size all need attention as throughput grows.

The codebase itself carries its own friction: the ongoing migration from Scala core to Java modules means related logic is split across core, storage, and group-coordinator (the Scala LogManager even aliases the Java one), and two live consumer protocols mean any client-behavior reading must check which delegate is actually running. None of that diminishes the engineering here — it is just the price of a system that has been evolving this fast for this long, and reading the sources on trunk, as we did here, is the most reliable way to know what your cluster is really doing.

entry.title: Meilisearch Source Tour: How the Rust Search Engine Works Under the Hood

link.title: Meilisearch Source Tour: How the Rust Search Engine Works Under the Hood

entry.content:
Meilisearch is one of those projects that feels deceptively small from the outside. You POST some JSON documents to it, you POST a query, and half a second later you get typo-tolerant, ranked results with facet counts. Under the hood, though, it is a carefully layered Rust system: an HTTP layer built on actix-web, an asynchronous task scheduler that persists every write to LMDB before acknowledging it, and a search engine crate called milli that owns inverted indexes, facet databases, and vector stores. This post is a source tour of that system, based on a fresh read of the repository at its default main branch.

The layout itself tells you a lot before you read a single function. Everything lives under crates/: crates/meilisearch is the HTTP server you actually launch, crates/index-scheduler is the durable work queue, and crates/milli is the engine core with no knowledge of HTTP at all. That separation is deliberate — milli could be reused by a different frontend entirely, which is exactly what makes the codebase pleasant to navigate. If you have read our earlier tours of Elasticsearch or the pure-Rust Tantivy library, you will notice Meilisearch sits between the two philosophies: more opinionated and turnkey than Tantivy, far lighter than Elasticsearch.

Two diagrams accompany this post. The overview shows the three crates and the main arrows between HTTP handlers, the scheduler, and the engine. The detail diagram goes one level down into the scheduler’s batch creation and milli’s ranking-rule machinery. Every node in the interactive SVG links to the real file on GitHub, so you can keep this page open in one tab and the source in another.

Meilisearch at a glance: the actix-web REST layer turns every write into a queued task, the index-scheduler applies batches to milli, and search reads milli directly. Click any node to open its source file.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at main.rs setup, which parses the Opt configuration, wires tracing, and starts the actix HTTP server. The application itself is assembled by create_app, L137, and setup_meilisearch, L220 constructs the scheduler and auth controller that every handler shares.
  • Index lifecycle endpoints live in one module: create_index, L231 on POST /indexes, plus get, update and delete handlers in the same file.
  • Document writes are handled by replace_documents, L1367, which delegates to the shared document_addition, L1534 helper. Crucially, this handler returns HTTP 202 Accepted — the write has only been enqueued.
  • The enqueuing point is IndexScheduler::register, L930 in the index-scheduler crate, which persists a Task into an LMDB-backed Queue, L129.
  • On the read path, search_with_post, L866 deserializes a SearchQuery, L87 struct and calls perform_search, L1852 synchronously — search never goes through the task queue.
  • The scheduler resolves which physical database a request touches through IndexMapper, L60, which opens and caches per-index LMDB environments.
  • Each index is a milli::Index, L131: a bundle of LMDB databases for word-to-document postings, exact-attribute postings, synonyms, prefix databases, facet trees, and vectors.
  • Query execution bottoms out in milli’s execute_search, L809, with a parallel execute_vector_search, L744 path for hybrid and semantic queries backed by the vector store.

One subtlety worth calling out before the detail diagram: the search path deliberately bypasses the scheduler entirely. Reads run synchronously against the LMDB environment with bounded concurrency — crates/meilisearch/src/search_queue.rs implements a permit-based queue whose capacity you can tune, and main.rs passes it into the app state. Writes, by contrast, always funnel through the task queue even for tiny updates. This asymmetry is the whole design in one sentence: reads are cheap and direct, writes are durable and serialized. It also explains a common beginner surprise — you POST a hundred documents and immediately search for one of them and get nothing back. The task was accepted, not applied; wait for the scheduler to drain its batch and the document appears.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps the onboarding honest: three steps and you have search. First, get an instance — either the hosted cloud offering or a self-hosted binary. Locally, the fastest route is the official install script, which downloads a single static binary:

curl -L https://install.meilisearch.com | sh
./meilisearch

Docker works just as well if you prefer containers: docker run -it --rm -p 7700:7700 -v $(pwd)/meili_data:/meili_data getmeili/meilisearch:latest. With no master key set, the local instance runs in an unrestricted dev mode; setting MEILI_MASTER_KEY switches on the API-key security layer implemented in crates/meilisearch-auth.

Second, add documents. The example from the README creates an index called movies implicitly and sends three records:

curl -X POST "http://localhost:7700/indexes/movies/documents" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary '[
    { "id": 1, "title": "Carol", "genres": ["Romance", "Drama"] },
    { "id": 2, "title": "Wonder Woman", "genres": ["Action", "Adventure"] },
    { "id": 3, "title": "Life of Pi", "genres": ["Adventure", "Drama"] }
  ]'

The response is a JSON object with a taskUid, and this is the moment the architecture we just mapped becomes visible: your curl hit replace_documents, which enqueued a DocumentAddition task and returned immediately. Indexing happens in the background. Poll GET /tasks/{taskUid} until the status flips to succeeded, then issue the third request, a search:

curl -X POST "http://localhost:7700/indexes/movies/search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary '{ "q": "wondre woman" }'

Meilisearch returns Wonder Woman despite the typo in wondre. That is not a gimmick — typo tolerance is a first-class ranking rule computed against the prefix and exact-posting databases you saw in the Index struct. From Python this same flow takes three lines with the meilisearch client package, which makes the engine a natural companion for FastAPI backends and retrieval-augmented applications — add a dedicated vector store only when you need heavier semantic search alongside keyword search.

How Indexing Actually Happens

The scheduler is the most interesting subsystem for anyone writing concurrent services in Rust. Its run loop lives in a dedicated thread (run, L630) and each iteration executes a tick, L168. A tick reads newly registered tasks, groups compatible ones via create_next_batch, L540, and hands the batch to process_batch, L53. Because tasks are persisted in LMDB before the HTTP response is sent, a crash between “accepted” and “indexed” loses nothing — on restart the scheduler replays the queue. This design is why the API can promise asynchronous durability without a separate message broker.

Inside process_batch, document additions reach milli’s write side. The merged change set flows into the parallel indexer entry point extract, L99, which fans extraction work across rayon threads: field ids, word docids, facet values, and — when the index settings declare embedders — document embeddings. Settings changes travel the same road: the update_all, L577 settings handler enqueues a SettingsUpdate task, and the scheduler re-indexes the affected data. This is also where tokenization enters: milli delegates segmentation and normalization to the charabia crate (declared in crates/milli/Cargo.toml), which gives the engine its multi-language coverage including Chinese, Japanese, Hebrew and Latin-script languages.

Search Execution Inside milli

On the read side, perform_search translates the HTTP query into a SearchContext and calls into milli. extract_tokens, L909 splits the user query into terms and builds a query graph — a small DAG of possible words including typo variants. execute_search, L809 then resolves the candidate universe and asks get_ranking_rules_for_query_graph_search, L510 to assemble the rule chain: words, typo, proximity, attribute, sort, and exactness, mirroring the documented default ranking order. If the request carries a sort parameter, resolve_sort_criteria, L651 inserts the sort rules ahead of the relevance rules.

Worth a brief mention too is the federation layer above all of this: the same crates/meilisearch/src/search/federated/ module powers the multi-search endpoint, where one HTTP request fans out into per-index queries and merges the responses with weighted scores. In network mode it can even forward sub-queries to remote Meilisearch instances, which is the project’s answer to read scaling without full distribution. None of that machinery lives in milli — it is pure HTTP-layer composition on top of perform_search, which keeps the engine crate simple and the composability at the API level where it belongs.

Facets are computed by FacetDistribution, L84, which walks the facet-number and facet-string databases restricted to the result universe. For hybrid queries — where the client sends both q and an embedder reference in the request body — execute_vector_search queries the ANN-enabled vector store and merges semantic and keyword candidates through the score-merging logic in crates/meilisearch/src/search/federated/. The detail diagram traces both of these paths end to end:

The detailed view: task registration and batch creation on the scheduler side, ranking-rule construction and facet distribution on the search side, and the parallel extraction stages on the write side.

Honest Limits

Meilisearch makes deliberate trade-offs, and the README is upfront about several of them. It is a single-binary, single-node engine: there is no built-in distributed cluster, and scaling past one machine means using the experimental network/federated search features or sharding yourself. The dataset fits where LMDB fits — indexes live on your local disk, so very large corpora need multiple instances or a distributed engine like Elasticsearch. Note also that LMDB caps the read transaction count, which is precisely why crates/meilisearch/src/search_queue.rs exists to throttle concurrent searches. Async indexing is a feature, but it means writes are not immediately visible — clients must poll tasks, which adds a bit of bookkeeping compared to synchronous engines like Typesense. Finally, benchmark figures in the README (sub-50-millisecond searches, etc.) are the project’s own claims measured on its own workloads under workloads/; treat them as directional, not as independent results. For pure algorithmic detail on inverted indexing in Rust, Tantivy remains the deeper rabbit hole, and for end-to-end local chat-plus-search stacks you can wire an Open WebUI retrieval layer in front of Meilisearch yourself.
