entry.title: MinIO Under the Hood: How a Go Object Store Turns Disks into an S3 Cloud

link.title: MinIO Under the Hood: How a Go Object Store Turns Disks into an S3 Cloud

entry.content:
Modern AI and data workloads live and die by storage. Training corpora, checkpoints, dataset shards, model weights, Parquet lakes, backup archives — all of it eventually lands in object storage because that is the one abstraction every tool agrees on. The S3 API became the lingua franca: Spark reads from it, MLflow stores artifacts in it, and Kubernetes operators mount it for everything from logs to datasets. When you need that API on your own hardware — for cost, for data locality, for compliance — MinIO is the open source answer that has defined the category for a decade.

MinIO is written in Go, ships as a single binary, and speaks the S3 API natively rather than emulating it through a translation layer. Point any S3 SDK or the mc client at a MinIO endpoint and it just works. But the genuinely interesting part is underneath the API surface: MinIO takes a pile of ordinary disks (or a fleet of ordinary servers) and turns them into a single highly available namespace that survives disk failures, host failures, and even the silent bit-level rot that plagues long-lived drives. It does this with Reed-Solomon erasure coding, a custom on-disk metadata format, and a quorum-based distributed lock service — all implemented from scratch in the repo we are walking through today.

This post is a source tour of minio/minio at its default branch (master, commit 7aac2a2c5b7c). We traced the request path from the HTTP edge down to the raw disk driver, verified every symbol and line number, and drew two architecture maps. The overview shows the big layers; the detail map goes one level deeper into erasure mechanics, locking, and cluster messaging.

Overview: from the S3 router at the edge, through the ObjectLayer contract and the pool/set topology, down into the Reed-Solomon engine, the per-disk XL storage layer, and the namespace lock service.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at registerAPIRouter, L255, where every S3 endpoint is mounted on a mux router, guarded by s3APIMiddleware, L210. The objectAPIHandlers struct that carries all handler state is defined right there at L68.
  • The write path funnels into PutObjectHandler, L1793, which authenticates, parses headers, streams the body, and calls the backend; reads come back through GetObjectHandler, L717 and HeadObjectHandler, L1012.
  • Both handlers speak to the backend only through the ObjectLayer interface, L246 — a clean seam that lets the same HTTP layer serve single-node and clustered deployments.
  • At boot, serverMain, L746 validates the endpoint list and calls newObjectLayer, L1199, which returns a running backend wired into the global server state.
  • The backend is a stack: erasureServerPools, L52 federates one or more pools, newErasureSets, L352 carves each pool into sets of disks, and the hash placement function hashOrder, L178 decides which disk in a set owns which shard.
  • Object operations execute inside a set: PutObject, L1249 drives encoding and parallel shard writes, while GetObjectNInfo, L203 reassembles data even when some disks are offline.
  • Finally, every shard lands on xlStorage, L98, the per-disk driver whose WriteAll, L2305 and CreateFile, L2092 methods are where bytes actually meet the filesystem, with object metadata persisted in the xlMetaV2 format at L901.

The detail map below adds the machinery the overview abstracts away: multipart upload state, healing, bitrot checksums, the distributed lock stack, peer-to-peer RPC, and the configuration/crypto subsystems.

Detail view: handlers, the object layer, the erasure engine, XL storage, quorum locking via DRWMutex and dsync, grid-based peer messaging, and the config/KMS layer.

From Install to Your First Object

MinIO’s README is refreshingly blunt about its distribution model these days: the community edition ships as source code only, and the recommended install is a one-liner:

go install github.com/minio/minio@latest

You need Go 1.24 or newer. Once the binary exists, starting a server is exactly what you would hope: minio server PATH, where PATH is any empty folder. On first boot the server comes up with default root credentials minioadmin:minioadmin, and the embedded web console is available at http://127.0.0.1:9000 — from there you can create buckets and upload objects with a browser. That single-folder mode is not a toy: it is the same code path — the same xlStorage driver and erasure machinery, just with one disk — that a fifty-node cluster runs.

To exercise the S3 API properly, grab the MinIO Client (mc) and run:

mc alias set local http://localhost:9000 minioadmin minioadmin
mc admin info local
mc mb local/data
mc cp ~/Downloads/mydata local/data/

That is the full loop: alias the endpoint, inspect the deployment, create a bucket, and copy real files in. Everything mc does here translates to ordinary S3 REST calls hitting the handlers in the diagram above — mc mb ends up at PutBucketHandler, L720, and mc cp ends up at PutObjectHandler. For container users, the README documents building a local image with docker build . and running it as docker run -p 9000:9000 -p 9001:9001 myminio:minio server /tmp/minio --console-address :9001, exposing both the S3 API and the console port. For anything beyond a laptop, the same binary expands horizontally: list multiple hosts and disks on the command line, and MinIO forms pools and sets across them — no separate “coordinator” process to install. Teams that run Kubernetes can pair it with the official MinIO Operator, and it slots naturally next to other self-hosted infrastructure we have covered, from Kubernetes itself to a Hugging Face Hub mirror for model artifacts.

How Erasure Coding Actually Works

The heart of MinIO is not a database or a journal — it is a Reed-Solomon codec. The Erasure struct, L35 holds a data-shard count, a parity-shard count, and a block size, and NewErasure, L42 sanity-checks the parameters (at most 256 shards) before lazily constructing a klauspost/reedsolomon encoder. On a write, Erasure.Encode, L69 streams the object in blocks, splitting each block into data shards and computing parity shards, then fans the shards out to per-disk writers in parallel. Because the code is systematic, data shards are directly readable and parity shards are pure insurance: with 8 data and 4 parity shards per set, any 8 of the 12 disks can reconstruct the object.

Placement is deterministic rather than replicated. hashOrder, L178 hashes the object name into a shuffle of disk indexes, and newFileInfo, L388 records that distribution in the object’s metadata, so every process in the cluster computes the same answer for “where does shard 3 live”. Reads go through Erasure.Decode, L239, which wraps multiple disk readers in a parallelReader and pulls from whichever disks respond fastest, tolerating absent or corrupt shards as long as the read quorum holds.

Two quieter pieces make this production-grade. First, bitrot protection: bitrot-streaming.go wraps every shard in a streaming hash, so silent corruption on any drive is detected at read time instead of being served to users. Second, healing: HealObject, L1060 notices stale or missing shards, reads the surviving ones, re-encodes through Erasure.Heal, L317, and rewrites the damaged disks in place. Together these give MinIO the durability story that a naive “replicate three times” design struggles to match at the same disk cost.

The Storage Layer Beneath

Below the erasure engine sits the XL storage layer, one xlStorage instance per disk. Its methods are deliberately boring — ReadAll, L1829, WriteAll, L2305, CreateFile, L2092, RenameFile, L2997 — because all the intelligence lives above it. Each object is stored as its shard files plus a metadata blob named xl.meta, formatted by xlMetaV2, L901. That format is version-aware: a single xl.meta can carry multiple object versions, per-part information for multipart uploads, checksum records, and inline data for small objects, which lets tiny objects be served without extra file reads.

Metadata correctness is enforced by quorum, not by a leader. erasure-metadata.go implements functions like findFileInfoInQuorum, L289 that gather FileInfo answers from all disks in a set and accept only what a majority agrees on, with helpers like ObjectToPartOffset, L268 translating byte ranges into shard reads. Disk health is probed through calls like CheckParts, L2399. This metadata-is-data philosophy — the same erasure machinery protects object bytes and metadata alike — keeps the system self-describing after any crash.

Locks, Peers, and Cluster Consistency

Object storage looks embarrassingly parallel until two clients race on the same key. MinIO serializes this with a three-tier lock stack. Locally, namespace-lock.go builds an in-process nsLockMap (via newNSLock, L66) that merges concurrent lockers for the same resource. Cluster-wide, the DRWMutex type at L113 of internal/dsync/drwmutex.go implements distributed read/write locks that require a quorum of N/2+1 grants — Lock, L158 blocks until enough remote lockers say yes, and a refresh loop keeps the grant alive during long operations. The quorum negotiation itself lives in internal/dsync, against the NetLocker interface, L23.

Those lockers are wired to real endpoints by newLockAPI, L101, one stub per peer host, and served on the far side by LockHandler, L52. Note what is not here: no ZooKeeper, no etcd, no external consensus service. All intra-cluster messaging — locks, peer REST calls, notifications between nodes — rides on internal/grid, a connection manager that multiplexes typed RPC streams between nodes. The client side of that mesh is peer-rest-client.go (its grid wiring is visible around L49), and the server side is peer-rest-server.go. It is a textbook example of a Go project betting on simple, self-contained primitives.

Where MinIO Fits in an AI Stack

For ML work, MinIO is usually the quiet dependency underneath everything else. It backs artifact stores — point MLflow at an S3 endpoint and every run’s models and metrics land in MinIO buckets. It holds datasets, index snapshots, and analytic extracts that feed engines like ClickHouse, and it gives long-running training jobs a durable place to checkpoint. The design choices we traced above are exactly why: the S3 API means no bespoke client code, versioning means experiments are reproducible, and erasure coding means a disk loss during a week-long training run is an operations ticket rather than a research incident.

Honest Limits

The most important caveat is the one MinIO states itself: as of the current README, the community edition is distributed as source code only, with no maintained pre-compiled binary releases — legacy binaries exist but “will not receive updates”. If you do not maintain a Go toolchain, the Docker-build path becomes the practical route, and production use of self-compiled binaries is explicitly at your own risk under AGPLv3, which also has licensing implications for some commercial embedded uses. Second, this is real distributed systems software: the quorum locking and pool/set topology demand that you think about server counts, drive counts, and network reliability up front; a two-node “cluster” with one dead node is not degraded, it is read-only, by quorum design. Third, capacity planning matters: objects in a set are striped across that set’s disks, so unbalanced sets or pools of very different ages will show uneven utilization — the pool-routing code picks where new objects land, but it cannot rewrite history. Finally, while MinIO is S3-compatible in the ways almost everyone uses, it is not a bit-for-bit S3 clone; exotic IAM corner cases and some newer AWS-only features may behave differently, so test the SDK paths your application actually exercises. None of these are hidden, but they belong in any evaluation.

entry.title: ParadeDB Source Tour: How pg_search Turns Postgres into a Tantivy-Powered Search Engine

link.title: ParadeDB Source Tour: How pg_search Turns Postgres into a Tantivy-Powered Search Engine

entry.content:
Most teams that need full-text search eventually make an uncomfortable choice: keep everything in Postgres and accept the limits of its built-in text search, or stand up a separate engine like Elasticsearch and figure out how to keep two copies of the data consistent. ParadeDB, the repository behind the paradedb/paradedb GitHub organization, makes a third bet — embed a real search engine inside Postgres itself. The project’s tagline is blunt about it: “Just use Postgres. One Postgres for your application data, full-text search, vector retrieval, and aggregations.”

The implementation lives in the pg_search extension, a Rust crate compiled against pgrx that embeds Tantivy — the same Lucene-inspired library that powers Meilisearch-style engines — directly into the Postgres backend process. On top of that engine sits a custom index access method, a SQL-visible @@@ search operator, a planner hook that reroutes queries into a parallel custom scan, and MVCC-aware segment storage that survives Postgres crashes. Apache DataFusion joins the picture for aggregate workloads.

This post is a guided tour of that source tree as of October 2026, based on the main branch. Rather than describe the project from its documentation, we traced the actual code paths: what happens at CREATE EXTENSION, what runs when you write CREATE INDEX ... USING paradedb, and how a WHERE description @@@ 'running shoes' clause becomes a Tantivy query and then rows in your result set. Two diagrams map the moving parts — a high-level overview first, then a deeper walkthrough of the reader, writer, and storage layers.

Overview of the pg_search extension: the extension entry point registers GUCs and the index access method; SQL-level predicates compile into executable query inputs; the access method's build, insert, and scan callbacks drive the embedded Tantivy engine.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • _PG_init, L127 is the extension’s entry point in pg_search/src/lib.rs. It runs when Postgres loads the shared library and wires up the planner machinery before any SQL is spoken.
  • gucs::init, L374 registers the paradedb.* session settings in gucs.rs — dozens of toggles covering custom scans, segment counts, parallelism thresholds, and cost heuristics.
  • bm25_handler, L111 is the index access method handler. It fills an IndexAmRoutine with function pointers for build, insert, scan, delete, and vacuum — this is the moment USING bm25 (and its newer alias USING paradedb) becomes a first-class Postgres index type.
  • ambuild, L38 implements CREATE INDEX: it reads every heap tuple, converts rows into Tantivy documents, and commits them as segments, with parallel builds supported on Postgres 17+.
  • aminsert, L227 keeps the index fresh on ordinary INSERTs. Each indexed row becomes a Tantivy document keyed by its heap ctid.
  • amgettuple, L293 and its bitmap sibling amgetbitmap, L346 are the two ways Postgres pulls matching rows out of the index during an index or bitmap scan.
  • register_planner_hook, L268 intercepts planning so that a search predicate is executed by a custom scan node instead of a generic index scan — the key to top-N ordering and parallel workers.
  • SerialIndexWriter, L211 is the single-writer wrapper around Tantivy that every mutation funnels through; commit, L522 makes written segments durable and visible.
  • SearchIndexReader, L588 opens an MVCC-consistent view of the committed segments and exposes the search, top-K, and estimation entry points used by both scan paths.

The next diagram zooms into the internals: the SQL surface with its pdb helper types, every access-method callback, the planner and custom-scan layer, the Tantivy reader and writer, and the segment storage they share.

Detailed view of pg_search internals. The access-method group shows the build, insert, scan, delete, and vacuum callbacks that `bm25_handler` wires into Postgres; every query shape funnels through `SearchQueryInput` before hitting the Tantivy reader; the writer commits segments that `MVCCDirectory` later exposes to snapshot-consistent readers.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest way to run ParadeDB is the bundled Docker image. The README’s one-liner is:

curl -fsSL https://paradedb.com/install.sh | sh

That script starts a container with the extension preloaded and drops you into a psql session. If you build from source instead, the repo is a standard pgrx workspace: cargo pgrx init to provision a Postgres install, then cargo pgrx install from the pg_search/ directory. Either way, the first SQL statement is the usual extension dance:

CREATE EXTENSION pg_search CASCADE;

The CASCADE matters — pg_search depends on companion extension objects for its pdb schema of helper types. Next, create a table and index it. Following the docs’ mock_items example:

CREATE TABLE mock_items (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    description TEXT,
    category TEXT,
    rating INTEGER
);

CREATE INDEX search_idx ON mock_items
USING paradedb (id, description, category);

A note on naming: version 0.25.0 renamed the index from “BM25 index” to “ParadeDB index” and added USING paradedb as the canonical access method name. USING bm25 still works as a backwards-compatible alias — both names resolve to the same bm25_handler C function in pg_search/src/postgres/mod.rs. Listing the columns inside the CREATE INDEX statement is how you select which fields become searchable; per-field tokenizers and filters are configured with the pdb.field(...) and pdb.tokenizer(...) option helpers you can see parsed in api/config.rs.

Then query it:

SELECT id, description, rating
FROM mock_items
WHERE description @@@ 'running shoes'
ORDER BY rating DESC
LIMIT 10;

The @@@ operator is the whole query language in one glyph. Its right-hand side can be a bare string, or a typed expression built from the pdb schema — pdb.bool_and, pdb.fuzzy, phrase queries with slop, boosts via pdb.boost, and so on. Scoring is BM25 by default, and you can select the score with paradedb.score(id) or get highlighted snippets back. Beyond plain search, the same index serves filters, facets, term aggregations, vector similarity, and even cross-table joins — which is why the 0.25.0 rename makes sense in context.

Inside the Index Access Method

The cleverest structural decision in the codebase is that ParadeDB is not a separate server talking to Postgres over a socket. It is a bona fide Postgres index access method — the same extension point that btree, hash, and GIN use. That is what bm25_handler registers, and it explains why CREATE INDEX ... USING paradedb looks exactly like any other Postgres DDL.

Each callback has a non-trivial story. ambuild calls into create_index at pg_search/src/postgres/build.rs L303, which reads BM25IndexOptions (L409 in postgres/options.rs) to turn index options into a Tantivy schema, then streams every heap tuple through the writer. Inserts go through aminsert and are batched; Postgres 17+ gets an aminsertcleanup callback (L397 in insert.rs) that finalizes the batch when the insert series ends, which also keeps logical replication correct. Deletions during VACUUM land in ambulkdelete (L96 in delete.rs), and amvacuumcleanup (L24 in vacuum.rs) schedules segment merges afterward.

The storage layer underneath is worth appreciating. Tantivy segments are stored on Postgres relation forks through a custom directory implementation — MVCCDirectory at L372 in index/directory/mvcc.rs gives each snapshot of the database a consistent view of which segments exist, so a long-running query never sees a segment that a concurrent transaction hasn’t committed, and a rollback can’t leave phantom segments behind. Segment merges are serialized by a MergeLock (L43 in postgres/storage/merge.rs) so two vacuum workers can’t merge the same segments twice.

Queries: From @@@ to Tantivy

When the planner sees a @@@ predicate, three layers cooperate. First, the SQL surface: the operator’s support functions in pg_search/src/api/operator.rs parse the right-hand side into a pdb::Query value (the typed DSL at L362 in query/pdb_query.rs) and rewrite the predicate into a SearchQueryInput — the central enum at L76 in pg_search/src/query/mod.rs that represents every executable query shape. Second, estimation: estimate_selectivity_and_cost (L780 in operator.rs) asks the reader for a fast doc-count estimate via estimate_docs (L2697 in index/reader/index.rs) so Postgres can cost the plan sanely. Third, execution: the planner hook replaces the plan with a custom scan that compiles the SearchQueryInput into Tantivy queries and runs them over the MVCC-visible segments.

Custom Scans and Top-K

Why not just answer from amgettuple? Because search workloads care about ordering. A web-style query is almost always “top 10 by relevance” or “top 10 by relevance with filters,” and a generic index scan would fetch every match and then sort. The BaseScan custom scan (L112 in postgres/customscan/basescan/mod.rs) instead runs a TopKScanExecState execution method (L63 in top_k.rs) that keeps a bounded heap of the best documents seen so far, often using “fast fields” (stored numeric columns inside the index) to avoid heap fetches entirely. The planner hook also drives aggregate custom scans built on DataFusion, parallel scans that split segments across workers, and a join custom scan for cross-table search predicates. All of these are individually switchable through the GUCs registered at startup.

Honest Limits

Some grounded observations from the docs and code, without invented benchmarks:

  • Not a standalone server. Tantivy runs inside each Postgres backend. You get ACID transactions and one system to operate, but heavy indexing work consumes the Postgres memory and CPU you give it; there are GUCs for writer memory budgets and background merging, but capacity planning is still your job.
  • Index the fields you query. Like any inverted index, only columns listed in the CREATE INDEX statement are searchable. The deprecated key_field option is accepted for compatibility but ignored — new indexes don’t need a designated key column.
  • Renaming churn is real. This repository moves fast: the 0.25.0 access-method rename, per-version migration files from 0.15.x through 0.26.x, and frequent option changes mean pin versions and read the changelog before upgrading.
  • Version floor matters. Current examples in the docs assume ParadeDB 0.26.0 or newer, and some parallel features require Postgres 17 or 18.
  • License. The community edition is AGPL-3.0, with enterprise features commercially licensed — relevant if you embed it in a service.

For context on where this design sits in the ecosystem, ParadeDB is best read alongside the tools it borrows from and competes with: the embedded Tantivy engine we covered in our Tantivy source tour, the classic standalone architecture of Elasticsearch, and the vector-only Postgres extension pgvector, which ParadeDB complements with hybrid search — BM25 and vector similarity from the same index.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of the paradedb/paradedb repository: BM25 indexes, the @@@ operator, custom scans, and the Rust/Tantivy engine inside Postgres.

entry.title: Prometheus in Go: How the Monitoring Engine Behind Modern Infrastructure Actually Works

link.title: Prometheus in Go: How the Monitoring Engine Behind Modern Infrastructure Actually Works

entry.content:
If you run GPU boxes for training, serve models behind inference gateways, or orchestrate batch jobs across a cluster, you already know the uncomfortable truth: things fail silently unless something is watching. A saturated NVLink, a queue that stops draining, a worker that leaks memory for six hours before the OOM killer arrives — none of these page you by themselves. That is exactly the gap a metrics system fills, and the de facto standard for filling it is Prometheus, the CNCF project that has become the connective tissue of cloud-native observability. When you pair it with dashboards or hook it into a Kubernetes deployment, every node, pod and GPU exporter in your fleet becomes a queryable time series.

What makes Prometheus interesting from a code perspective is that it is not a thin orchestrator gluing together other databases. It is a self-contained, single-binary system written in Go that ships its own time series database (TSDB), its own query language engine (PromQL), its own pull-based collection machinery, and its own rule evaluator for recording and alerting. Everything from the write-ahead log on disk to the AST evaluator that computes rate() over your metrics lives in one repository. For ML infrastructure teams, that matters: your training cluster metrics are stored in a format you can actually read the source code of, and the storage cost model is local disk, not a metered cloud service.

In this post we walk through the actual source of prometheus/prometheus on the main branch and map how the pieces fit together: the entry point in cmd/prometheus, the scrape manager, the TSDB write path, block compaction, the PromQL engine, rule evaluation, and the web API that ties it all together. Every function and line number below was verified directly against the checked-out source, and the two diagrams are generated from the real call structure. If you later want to give these metrics a SQL-flavored home for long-horizon analytics, our TimescaleDB tour is a natural companion read; for dashboards on top, see Grafana.

Overview: one Go binary wires the web API, scrape manager, rule manager and TSDB together at startup; scrapes feed the head block through the WAL, and compaction drains the head into immutable blocks that the query engine reads back.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main() at cmd/prometheus/main.go, L389 parses flags — the config file defaults to prometheus.yml (L434) and the listen address to 0.0.0.0:9090 (L443) — then opens storage and starts every subsystem below it.
  • scrape.NewManager at scrape/manager.go, L52 builds the collection side; its Run loop, L223 consumes target sets that service discovery produces and reconciles one scrape loop per target.
  • scrapeLoop.run at scrape/scrape.go, L1404 is the per-target heartbeat: on every interval tick it calls scrapeAndReport, L1487, which fetches /metrics, decodes the payload, and even synthesizes the famous up metric when a target misbehaves.
  • DB.Appender at tsdb/db.go, L1366 is the single write entrance; it wraps the head block’s transactional appender so that both scrape loops and rule evaluations funnel into the same path.
  • WL.Log at tsdb/wlog/wlog.go, L657 writes each batch into the write-ahead log before the sample is considered durable — this is why a crash costs you seconds of data, not the whole head.
  • Engine at promql/engine.go, L519 is the PromQL evaluator; exec, L1091 drives each query from AST down to storage reads.
  • rules.Manager at rules/manager.go, L121 owns rule groups; each Group.Eval at rules/group.go, L504 runs on its own interval and pushes results straight back into storage.

Detailed view: the write path (scrape to WAL to head), the compaction path (head to leveled blocks), the read path (API to engine to queriers over head and blocks), and the rule loop that closes the circle.

From Install to Your First Query

The README keeps getting-started deliberately short, and we verified every claim here against it. The fastest route is the official Docker image: docker run --name prometheus -d -p 127.0.0.1:9090:9090 prom/prometheus, after which the README states Prometheus is reachable at http://localhost:9090/. If you prefer binaries, precompiled releases are on the prometheus.io download page, and building from source requires the Go version pinned in go.mod plus NodeJS for the web UI, then either go install github.com/prometheus/prometheus/cmd/... or make build followed by ./prometheus --config.file=your_config.yml.

Configuration is a single YAML file. The README links an example at documentation/examples/prometheus.yml, and the minimal shape most people start with is a global section setting scrape_interval and a scrape_configs list. Each job declares a static_configs block (or relies on one of dozens of service-discovery integrations); the agent side of that bargain is the Target type in scrape/target.go, L63, which resolves the final scrape URL, L234 and carries the label set that will identify the series forever.

For a first query, open the UI and evaluate up — you should see one series per target with a value of 1. From there the natural next steps are rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total[5m]) for CPU burn, or max_over_time(node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes[1h]) when a training host looks sluggish. Each of those goes through the exact engine path we dissect next. And if your fleet is containerized, the same scrape model extends cleanly to a Kubernetes cluster via pod annotations or its discovery mechanisms.

The Write Path: WAL First, Memory Second

When the process starts, Open at tsdb/db.go, L919 opens the data directory, loads persisted blocks, and rebuilds the head by replaying the log — Head.loadWAL at tsdb/head_wal.go, L82 reconstructs series and samples from WAL records so startup survives restarts. The head itself is built by NewHead at tsdb/head.go, L308 and exposed as the Head struct, L72: an in-memory map of series with memory-mapped chunks for older stretches.

Writes arrive as small transactions. Head.Appender at tsdb/head_append.go, L173 hands out an appender, and each call to headAppender.Append, L444 performs series lookup-or-create, ordering checks, and chunk encoding. The WAL wrapper (WL struct at tsdb/wlog/wlog.go, L182) is created with NewSize, L300, which fixes the segment size; WL.Log, L657 then pages, compresses and flushes records. The design point to remember: durability is cheap here because a WAL record is bytes, not an index update — the expensive indexing happens in memory and is rebuilt on replay.

One detail that shows how battle-tested this code is: the head keeps a bounded out-of-order window so late-arriving samples from a slow or retried scrape can still land correctly, a necessity when your scrape targets include network hops across a training cluster.

Compaction: From Head to Immutable Blocks

The head cannot grow forever. On a background cycle DB.Compact at tsdb/db.go, L1560 cuts the head into a block and then evaluates retention deletions. The strategy object behind this is the Compactor interface at tsdb/compact.go, L54, whose default implementation is the LeveledCompactor struct, L80, constructed through NewLeveledCompactor, L201. It merges blocks into progressively larger time ranges — by default the first level is two hours (DefaultBlockDuration at tsdb/db.go, L57), and the default retention configured in DefaultOptions at tsdb/db.go, L83 is 15 days (L87).

Blocks are immutable once written, which is what makes reads and backups tractable: a block is a directory with an index, chunk files and metadata, and queries reach it through the BlockReader interface at tsdb/block.go, L146. This layering — mutable head, immutable blocks, log in between — is the same conceptual shape you find in Redis persistence or log-structured stores, and it is why Prometheus can absorb tens of thousands of samples per second on commodity hardware without tuning.

How PromQL Evaluation Actually Works

The query side starts at Engine at promql/engine.go, L519, constructed by NewEngine, L568 with EngineOpts that bound sample counts and per-query timeout. The web API builds queries through two entry points: NewInstantQuery, L788 for a single timestamp and NewRangeQuery, L835 for start/end/interval evaluation. Both funnel into exec, L1091, which sets up query bookkeeping, and then into execEvalStmt, L1257, which opens storage queriers and walks the parsed AST with an evaluator.

The practical consequence: every vector selector in your expression becomes a series fetch against both the head (for recent samples) and persisted blocks (for history). Queries that scan wide label spaces pay for it in memory, which is why the MaxSamples guard exists. On the serving side, requests arrive at the v1 API (API struct at web/api/v1/api.go, L241): the instant handler query, L625 and the range handler queryRange, L1201 are registered on the router at L480-481, and the whole surface is mounted by the Handler in web/web.go, L222, whose serving loop lives in Run, L748.

Rules: Recording and Alerting

Rule files let you precompute expressions and define alerts. rules.NewManager at rules/manager.go, L172 builds the manager (Manager struct, L121); config reloads call Update, L271, which swaps in the new group set atomically. Each Group at rules/group.go, L45 runs its own goroutine (L208) on its configured interval, and Group.Eval, L504 evaluates rules in order so recording rules can feed alerts downstream.

Two rule kinds exist. RecordingRule at rules/recording.go, L39 evaluates an expression and writes the result as a new series (Eval, L86) — this is how you precompute expensive aggregations for dashboards. AlertingRule at rules/alerting.go, L116 runs the same evaluation but maintains a pending/firing state machine with for-clause tracking, and those states are exported as ALERTS series. For ML ops specifically, recording rules are the pragmatic answer to “what was p95 GPU memory across the fleet over the last hour” without re-aggregating raw series on every dashboard load — and they pair naturally with a scheduled retraining flow like the one we describe in the Airflow tour.

Honest Limits

Prometheus is deliberately not a distributed database. It is a single-node store by design: there is no built-in replication or sharding, and the project itself points users who need horizontal scale or long-term storage toward external systems (Thanos, Cortex, Mimir) that sit on top of it. If your retention ambition is measured in years, plan for object-storage-backed federation early rather than after your local disk fills.

Second, the pull model presumes scrapeable targets. Short-lived batch jobs — a five-minute training epoch, a one-off evaluation run — can finish before any scrape happens; the standard mitigation is a push gateway or converting job metrics into counters emitted by a longer-lived sidecar. Third, cardinality is the real operational cliff: every unique label combination is a series in memory and on disk, so an unbounded label like user_id or a full stack trace attached as a label will take the head down with it. Finally, PromQL is purpose-built for metrics math, not full-text logs or traces — it will not replace your log store, and trying to bend it into one is a common rookie mistake. None of these limits are bugs; they are the explicit trade-offs that keep the single binary fast, and the source we walked through shows exactly where each boundary is enforced.

entry.title: Redis Under the Hood: A Guided Tour of the C Source Behind the World’s Favorite In-Memory Database

link.title: Redis Under the Hood: A Guided Tour of the C Source Behind the World’s Favorite In-Memory Database

entry.content:
If you have ever cached an LLM response, rate-limited an API, or served precomputed features to a model at inference time, there is a very good chance Redis was sitting somewhere in the request path. Because the dataset lives in memory and is served by hand-tuned C data structures, reads and writes routinely land in the sub-millisecond range — exactly the budget a machine-learning service has left over after the model takes its share of the latency. That combination has made Redis the default hot layer of the AI stack: embeddings lookups, feature stores, session state, token-bucket counters, and leaderboard-style rankings all fit its model of “keep it in RAM, make every operation O(1) or O(log N)”.

The redis/redis repository on GitHub is the home of the open-source Redis codebase: a compact, deeply readable C project whose src/ directory contains essentially the entire server. Everything lives in one flat folder — the event loop, the client networking layer, every data type command, the snapshot and log writers, the replication engine, and the cluster bus protocol. There is almost nothing between you and the metal: just files with names like networking.c and t_zset.c that do exactly what they say.

This post is a guided tour of that source. The default development branch of the repository is unstable (the maintainers’ rolling tip; releases are cut from version branches), and every symbol and line number below was verified against that branch before publication. Two diagrams generated from the repository tree accompany the tour: an overview of the runtime architecture, and a denser detail map of the same code. One interesting wrinkle for 2026: the tree now bundles a modules/vector-sets directory — an HNSW-based similarity-search structure (vset.c, hnsw.c) that plugs the classic Redis command model into the vector-search workflow that tools like pgvector serve inside Postgres.

The runtime at a glance: a single-threaded event loop reads client commands, dispatches them to the data type implementations, and fans write commands out to the persistence layers and to replicas. Generated from the redis/redis tree, branch unstable.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The process starts conventionally. int main, L8369 parses configuration, initializes the databases and shared objects, and then hands control to the event loop.
  • The loop itself is aeMain, L497, a thin wrapper that repeatedly calls aeProcessEvents, L365, which polls sockets and timers through pluggable backends — the tree ships ae_epoll.c, ae_kqueue.c, ae_select.c, and ae_evport.c.
  • On every readable client socket the backend invokes readQueryFromClient, L4004, which appends bytes to the client’s query buffer, and processInputBuffer, L3801, which parses the RESP framing into an argv array.
  • Parsing hands off to processCommand, L4672, the dispatch gate that resolves the command table entry, checks authentication, arity, and key validity, then executes the command.
  • String operations run in setCommand, L430 and getCommand, L470; hashes in hsetCommand, L4257; sorted sets in zaddGenericCommand, L2250; lists in lpushCommand, L529.
  • Every write that succeeds is propagated by propagateNow, L3808 into two directions at once: the append-only log (via feedAppendOnlyFile, L1671) and the replication stream (via replicationFeedSlaves, L656).
  • Snapshots are taken by rdbSaveBackground, L2352, which forks a child process so the parent never stops serving traffic.

The detail map: the event loop internals, the RESP parsing path, ten command entry points across four data types, the RDB/AOF persistence machinery, the SYNC/PSYNC state machine, and the cluster gossip engine. Same tree, same branch, 34 nodes.

One Thread, One Loop, Zero Surprises

The most important architectural fact about Redis is what is not there: there is no lock table, no per-request thread, no connection worker pool. The main thread runs the event loop and does all client work; bioProcessBackgroundJobs, L261 is the exception that proves the rule — a small pool of worker threads for background jobs that must never block the loop: closing file descriptors, fsyncing the AOF, and lazily freeing large values. The job classes are created by bioCreateCloseJob, bioCreateFsyncJob, and bioCreateLazyFreeJob further up the file, and src/bio.c is only a few hundred lines long.

Between loop iterations, two hooks give the server its housekeeping rhythm. serverCron, L1581 runs on a timer and handles key expiration sampling, RDB save-point checks, and the cluster tick; beforeSleep, L1966 runs right before the loop blocks on I/O and does the latency-critical flushes — calling flushAppendOnlyFile and pushing pending replies out through handleClientsWithPendingWrites (both calls sit in its body, lines 1981–1982 and 2123). This split — fast bookkeeping when the loop is about to sleep — is a pattern worth stealing for any event-driven system you build.

The payoff of the single-threaded design is that every command is atomic without any locking protocol, which is precisely why INCR (incrCommand, L936) works as a distributed counter or rate limiter straight out of the box. The cost is equally clear: any command that blocks the loop blocks everyone, which is why blocking-list operations and slow disk work are the two places the codebase works hardest to defer.

Five Data Types, One Dispatch Table

Redis’s data type layer is a study in the encoding pattern: each logical type has several physical representations, chosen automatically by size. A hash starts life as a compact listpack and converts to a full dict when it grows; a sorted set flips from listpack to a skiplist-plus-dict pair at a threshold. The command implementations carry this logic inside themselves — genericHgetallCommand, L5601 iterates whichever encoding it finds, and zrangeGenericCommand, L4529 serves ZRANGE, ZREVRANGE, and their variants from one generic body. For a rank lookup, zrankGenericCommand, L4750 walks the skiplist’s width spans rather than counting elements one by one.

Lists ride on quicklist.c — a linked list of listpack nodes — which gives lpushCommand, L529 cheap head insertion while keeping memory dense. The blocking variants are the fun part: blpopCommand, L1375 parks the client on a “blocked clients” registry keyed by the awaited key, and a later push unblocks the waiter. That primitive is the backbone of countless job queues, including the worker hand-off schemes people build around batch inference services.

This dispatch-plus-encoding architecture is exactly what made the vector-sets addition feel native: a new type arrives with its own commands and its own encoding strategy (the HNSW graph in modules/vector-sets/hnsw.c), reusing the same command-table plumbing the string and hash commands have used since 2009. The similarity-search commands live in the bundled module (modules/vector-sets/vset.c), and the tree carries a full Python test suite for them under modules/vector-sets/tests/.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s build path is deliberately boring, and that is a feature. Clone the repository, then:

make -j "$(nproc)"
./src/redis-server redis.conf

make (equivalently make build / make all) builds the core server plus whatever is cloned under modules/. The binary lands in src/, and redis-cli is built alongside it — the README’s “Using Redis with redis-cli” section walks through connecting and issuing your first commands. If you only want the core data structures without the bundled modules’ toolchain (the modules bring heavier dependencies like LLVM, Rust, and CMake, installable via make bootstrap), the README notes the core-only alternative: build with make build redis and run ./src/redis-server with no config file.

From there the AI-flavored experiments need nothing but the primitives you have now met in the source. Cache model completions with SET/GET and a TTL; gate an endpoint with a token bucket built on INCR and expiry; index precomputed features in hashes and fetch a whole record with HGETALL; rank candidates in a sorted set and read the top slice with ZRANGE. If you installed the bundled modules, vector sets give you similarity search over embeddings without leaving the server — a lighter-weight sibling to the dedicated vector databases we covered in the pgvector tour. A common production pairing is Redis in front as the hot layer with a bulk store behind it — object storage like MinIO for checkpoints and raw corpora, or a columnar engine like ClickHouse for analytics — with Redis absorbing the per-request traffic that would otherwise hammer them.

One practical note before you ship any of this: source-built Redis is fast, but it is not a persistence miracle. Tune the AOF fsync policy to match your durability tolerance, and read the next section before betting correctness on snapshot timing. If your orchestration story needs cluster mode, size your key space with hash tags from day one.

Persistence: Two Insurance Policies

Redis offers two complementary durability mechanisms in clearly separate files. RDB snapshots (rdb.c) are point-in-time binaries: rdbSaveBackground, L2352 forks a child that serializes the dataset via the rio abstraction (rdbSaveRio at L2156) while the parent keeps serving; at startup, rdbLoad, L5396 restores the full state before the server accepts traffic. Forking is the trick — the child sees a frozen world thanks to copy-on-write, and the parent’s pause is limited to the fork itself.

AOF (aof.c) is the opposite trade: feedAppendOnlyFile, L1671 appends every propagated write to a log buffer, and flushAppendOnlyFile, L1409 — invoked from beforeSleep each loop cycle — writes and fsyncs it according to policy, sometimes deferring the fsync to the background threads through a bio job (the bioCreateFsyncJob call sits inside this function’s everysec path). When the log grows unwieldy, rewriteAppendOnlyFileBackground, L3291 forks a child that rebuilds the log from the current dataset, the same fork-and-freeze pattern as RDB. In practice most workloads run both: RDB for compact backups, AOF for bounded data loss on crash.

Replication and Cluster: Scaling Reads and Writes

Replication is a replica-pull protocol. A follower connects and issues SYNC or PSYNC, handled in syncCommand, L1213. If the follower’s offset is still inside the master’s replication backlog, masterTryPartialResynchronization, L1011 resumes the stream without a full copy; otherwise replicationSetupSlaveForFullResync, L951 schedules a BGSAVE handoff and ships the snapshot. From then on, replicationFeedSlaves, L656 appends every write to each replica’s output buffer — the same propagateNow fan-out you saw feeding the AOF.

Cluster mode shards the key space across nodes with the well-known 16384 hash slots: keys map to slots through CRC16 masked to 14 bits (see the slot helper at the top of src/cluster.c), and each node owns a slice of slots. The gossip engine lives in cluster_legacy.c: clusterCron, L4878 paces the protocol, clusterSendPing, L3827 pushes gossip messages over the bus, clusterProcessPacket, L2829 decodes incoming MEET/PING/PONG/FAIL traffic, and clusterUpdateSlotsConfigWith, L2389 remaps slot ownership when the topology changes. The common pieces — slot computation, DUMP/RESTORE, MIGRATE — sit in cluster.c itself, which the header describes as the parts shared between clustering implementations. This is the machinery for when a single hot cache outgrows one machine; for most AI services it is overkill until it very suddenly is not.

Honest Limits

  • RAM is the budget. Every byte you cache lives in memory, and the copy-on-write fork during BGSAVE or AOF rewrite can briefly double the footprint of a large dataset. Plan headroom, or use the lazy-free jobs to soften deletions.
  • Single-threaded means fairness matters. One expensive command — a huge key range, a runaway sort — delays every other client. The blocking primitives help queues, not compute-heavy scans.
  • Durability is a dial, not a guarantee. AOF everysec trades one second of writes on crash; RDB snapshots lose everything since the last save. The source makes the trade-offs legible, but you still choose them.
  • Cluster mode constrains your data model. Multi-key operations only work when keys share a slot (hash tags), and resharding moves real data. The 16384-slot design is elegant but opinionated.
  • The unstable branch moves. Line numbers here were verified against the tree at the time of writing; expect drift — the symbol names are far more durable than the line numbers.
  • Vector sets are young. The bundled modules/vector-sets module is new relative to the core types; treat it as promising but validate persistence and scaling for your workload before committing.

If this tour changes how you read Redis — from a black-box cache into a legible event-loop program with five data types bolted onto one dispatch table — it did its job. Pair it with the right bulk stores, and it remains the cheapest latency you will ever buy.
entry.summary: A verified line-by-line source tour of Redis: event loop, data type commands, persistence, replication, and cluster, mapped into two architecture diagrams.
